impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patent claims directed to humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's patents covering methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache, after a jury had found willful infringement and no invalidity. This decision is significant for the pharmaceutical industry as it addresses the scope of written description and enablement requirements for antibody patents claiming genus coverage based on functional characteristics.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for biologic drug manufacturers holding antibody patents with broad functional claims, reinforcing the enforceability of patents covering classes of therapeutic antibodies against competitors like Eli Lilly.
impacts.negativeImplications: Creates potential barriers for generic and biosimilar competitors seeking to challenge broad antibody patents on written description or enablement grounds, potentially delaying market entry of competing products.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights but retains the independent right to sue for infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the right to independently sue for infringement possesses a sufficient exclusionary right to satisfy Article III standing, even after granting an exclusive license for commercialization. This clarifies standing requirements in complex patent licensing arrangements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides significant flexibility for patent owners structuring licensing agreements, confirming they can retain enforcement rights and independently pursue infringers even after granting broad exclusive licenses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers may face patent infringement suits from patent owners who have licensed away most commercial rights but retained litigation rights, potentially complicating settlement and licensing negotiations.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was legally sufficient evidence to support the jury's finding that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding that the plaintiffs failed to establish that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed the patent invalidity finding, reasoning that generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions. The counterfeiting claim was affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity for businesses defending against trade secret claims by reinforcing that plaintiffs must demonstrate the asserted information is not generally known in the relevant field to qualify for trade secret protection.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face a heightened burden to demonstrate that their claimed secrets are not generally known, potentially undermining enforcement of trade secret portfolios that rely on combinations of known techniques.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices on farming equipment are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in declining to find the case exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, but vacated and remanded on the exceptionality determination for potential attorney fee awards. This decision is significant for agricultural technology companies and the broader software/data collection patent landscape.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent suits involving data collection and processing patents benefit from continued rigorous application of § 101 to abstract concepts, with the remand on exceptionality potentially enabling fee recovery in meritless patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: AgTech and IoT companies holding patents on data collection, processing, and sharing systems face continued vulnerability to § 101 challenges, limiting the enforceability of patents in these technology areas.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a verdict form containing a single infringement question covering multiple patents, without identifying which patent(s) were infringed, requires vacatur of the infringement and damages judgments, and whether the district court properly analyzed patent eligibility under Alice step two for the '495 patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated an $11.5 million patent infringement judgment and ordered a new trial because the verdict form improperly bundled infringement of four patents into a single question, making it impossible to determine which patents the jury found infringed. The court also remanded for further § 101 analysis. The ruling affirms that the '887 and '371 patents survive § 101 challenges.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides procedural safeguards for defendants by requiring patent-specific verdict forms in multi-patent cases, ensuring clarity in jury findings and protecting against overbroad damages awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders pursuing multi-patent infringement cases face greater procedural complexity and risk of vacatur if verdict forms do not separately address each patent, potentially increasing litigation costs.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly granted summary judgment of noninfringement of the '836 patent based on extraterritoriality and rejection of the doctrine of equivalents theory, and whether the court properly struck certain damages expert theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit addressed Intel's summary judgment of noninfringement on grounds of extraterritoriality and doctrine of equivalents for a multicore processor patent, reversing in part and remanding. The decision provides important guidance on the territorial limits of U.S. patent law as applied to semiconductor chip design and manufacturing processes that span multiple jurisdictions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Semiconductor and technology companies with global operations benefit from clarity on when overseas activities fall outside the reach of U.S. patent infringement claims under the extraterritoriality doctrine.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement against companies with multinational manufacturing and design operations may face difficulties establishing domestic infringement when key accused activities occur abroad.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages models and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award in a dispute over automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models. The court also reversed the district court's post-trial reduction of the jury's breach of contract damages award, reinstating the jury verdict. This decision is significant for software licensing disputes involving trade secret misappropriation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and licensors benefit from the reinstatement of jury contract damages and the instruction to reconsider broader damages theories, strengthening enforcement of trade secret and licensing rights.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies like Ford that develop internal software after licensing third-party technology face expanded damages exposure in trade secret misappropriation cases, with courts required to consider multiple damages methodologies.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Insulet's Defend Trade Secrets Act claim for misappropriation of insulin patch pump trade secrets was time-barred, where the alleged misappropriation began in 2018 and suit was filed in August 2023.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL, holding that Insulet's DTSA claim was barred by the three-year statute of limitations. Despite a jury verdict finding trade secret misappropriation and awarding damages, the court determined that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit. This decision significantly impacts trade secret enforcement timing.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides important protection for companies accused of trade secret misappropriation by strictly enforcing the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations, even where a jury finds liability on the merits.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face significant risk of losing claims if they delay filing suit, even when investigating or monitoring ongoing misappropriation, underscoring the need for prompt legal action upon discovery of potential theft.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC properly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement features violated Section 337 by infringing Masimo's patents covering wearable blood oxygen measurement devices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watches incorporating blood oxygen functionality covered by Masimo's patents, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation. The court found no error in the ITC's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings. This major decision impacts the wearable technology and medical device industries.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device patent holders like Masimo are affirmed in their ability to use ITC proceedings to enforce patents against major technology companies importing infringing products, with exclusion orders providing powerful remedies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies integrating health monitoring features into consumer products face significant risk of ITC exclusion orders that can block entire product lines from importation based on patent infringement findings.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge at summary judgment to establish prior art sales under the on-sale bar of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that 30(b)(6) witnesses may testify beyond personal knowledge at summary judgment and that computer source code is not hearsay. The decision addresses key evidentiary issues in patent validity challenges involving prior art products sold years before the patent priority date.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants challenging patent validity benefit from expanded evidentiary tools, as corporate representatives can testify about historical product sales without personal knowledge, and source code is admissible as non-hearsay evidence.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater exposure to invalidity challenges based on historical prior art sales, as defendants can rely on 30(b)(6) testimony from witnesses who joined the company after the relevant events occurred.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action when it previously missed the deadline for seeking a stay in its original declaratory judgment action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay by voluntarily dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action. This prevents gamesmanship in coordinating parallel ITC and district court proceedings and has significant implications for pharmaceutical patent litigation strategy.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders filing ITC complaints benefit from assurance that respondents cannot manipulate district court proceedings through tactical refiling to obtain mandatory stays they previously forfeited.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day deadline to seek a mandatory stay of parallel district court proceedings lose the ability to recover that right through refiling, potentially forcing them to litigate on two fronts simultaneously.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a specific temperature standard in the field, and whether the patent holder was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed no infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents, agreeing that the pH claim limitation must be measured at a temperature standard recognized in the field. The court also upheld the finding that Actelion was barred from asserting doctrine of equivalents. This decision impacts ANDA litigation strategies for pharmaceutical companies defending branded drug patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from precise claim construction that narrows branded drug patent scope, potentially enabling earlier market entry for generic competitors.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies with patents containing measurement-dependent claims face narrower patent protection when courts construe those measurements according to established industry standards rather than broader interpretations.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board erred in its obviousness determination of the challenged patent claims, and whether a non-party to district court litigation may file IPR petitions on behalf of or in coordination with a time-barred party under 35 U.S.C. § 315(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination for FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings, while declining to review the Board's refusal to terminate the IPR based on the time-bar issue. The case raises significant questions about the use of proxy IPR petitioners to challenge patents when the real party in interest is time-barred.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders gain some protection as the court vacated an adverse obviousness finding, and the case highlights potential limits on proxy IPR petitions filed by third parties to circumvent the one-year time bar.
impacts.negativeImplications: The court's refusal to review the time-bar termination issue leaves uncertainty about when third-party IPR petitions constitute impermissible circumvention of § 315(b), potentially enabling continued use of proxy challengers.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents are invalid for omission of a coinventor when the patent owner acknowledges coinventorship but cannot locate the omitted inventor to obtain consent for correction under 35 U.S.C. § 256.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that patents were invalid for failing to name all coinventors where the patent holder acknowledged an omitted foreign coinventor but could not locate him to complete the § 256 correction process. The court also denied judicial correction under § 256(b). This decision has significant implications for companies collaborating with foreign manufacturers on product development.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from this strict application of inventorship requirements, providing a defense when patent owners fail to properly name all contributors, particularly foreign collaborators.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that collaborate with foreign partners on product development face serious patent invalidation risk if they fail to properly document and name all inventors, especially when foreign contributors may become unreachable.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary charged excessive PACER fees, including the propriety of attorneys' fees and incentive awards to class representatives.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund projects beyond PACER's operation. The court upheld attorneys' fees, costs, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives. This decision impacts all regular users of federal court electronic records.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses and law firms that regularly access federal court records through PACER will receive refunds of overcharged fees, and the decision validates class action settlements involving government fee overcharges.
